utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody, and we welcome you back after the break. Good afternoon to you, sir. Would you please take the card and read aloud the affirmation that is on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Saxon will have some questions for you, but could I mention that you should not be too distracted by the microphones. It will be important for to you try and speak clearly so that everybody can hear you. If your voice is too quiet, it is not possible for the interpreters to pick up what you are saying. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Sir, is your name Blagoja Jakovoski?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And are you a citizen of the Republic of Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is your ethnicity Macedonian?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You work for the Ministry of the Interior of Macedonia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you please describe the career that you have had with the Ministry of the Interior. When did you begin your career?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: To put it briefly, since 1990, I started working in the Ministry of the Interior. I've been through several jobs, two or three, and I'm still with the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you first started your career, did you work as a uniformed police officer?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And after that, did you work in a Special Unit?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Posebna, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Posebna?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: It is similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at some point in time, in 2001, did you come to work as a security person or body-guard for Minister Ljube Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall when you took up that position?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't remember precisely what the date was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately. Can you give us a month perhaps.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I think it was May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And approximately for how long did you provide security for Mr. Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: For about two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now at that time, when you were providing security for Mr. Boskoski, were you a part of the sector of -- for security and protection of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you recall who was the head of that sector during the summer of 2001?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let me put it another way. Who was the chief of the minister's security unit or close protection unit?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Zoran Trajkovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, normally, who did you receive your orders from?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Always from Zoran Trajkovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So within the sector for security of the ministry, there was a chain of command that you followed. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would the same be true for your other colleagues in the sector for security?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct also.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Jakovoski, I forgot to ask you a question earlier. What is your current position within the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: At this moment, I'm inspector in violent crime, in Police Station Karpos.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. As a member of the close protection unit for Minister Boskoski, would it be fair to say that during 2001, or starting in May of 2001, you spent a lot of time in Minister Boskoski's presence?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes. One could say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you come to admire Minister Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I would fulfil my tasks professionally, upon the orders of Zoran Trajkovski, my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question is something different, inspector. My question is simply this, did you come to admire Minister Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I would always carry out my taskings professionally. I'm a professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, it's your duty to answer my questions today. I'd like an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Since he was my minister of the interior, he was my boss. I don't know how to answer this question, why. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What kind of qualities did Minister Boskoski have?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, first he was a good manager. He carried out well the tasks set forth by the prime minister. In his private life, he was a good parent, good person, in my opinion, a good father.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was he an effective minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What made Mr. Boskoski effective?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, whatever task he was given he would carry it out in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was he a determined person?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was Minister Boskoski a patriot?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't answer this question, patriot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was Minister --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was Minister Boskoski loyal to Macedonia and to the Macedonian people?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was Minister Boskoski loyal to the members of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was Minister Boskoski a brave person, in 2001?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In 2001, was Minister Boskoski willing to make sacrifices during the time of the crisis?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In 2001, did Minister Boskoski often share the risks of his police officers out in the field, out near the battlefields?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And as one of his close protection officers, did you sometimes accompany Minister Boskoski out to the combat areas?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When Minister Boskoski went out to the battlefield areas in 2001, did you ever go with him as his body-guard?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Of course. I was his body-guard. I would go with him. I did not accompany him. I was escorting him, guarding him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that correction, Inspector. I'd like to show you a document right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have some binders, and with the permission of the court usher, we have, I believe, copies for the Chamber and a copy to be given to the witness. And if Your Honours, could turn to what is marked as tab 1, and if Mr. Usher, if you could turn to the Macedonian version of tab 1 which is in the middle there. Your Honours, this is a book. It is entitled, "My Battle for Macedonia" and it was published by Ljube Boskoski in 2004. You do not have the entire English translation of the book in front of you. The Prosecution has managed to get portions of the book translated. And it is some of these portions which the Prosecution hopes to review with the witness this afternoon. Mr. Usher, do you need my assistance? Would you like me to help you out? And this is Rule 65 ter number four. I'm sorry, I didn't tell the court usher there -- I'm sorry, the court officer. The Macedonian version begins here. Okay. And if could you stay with the witness, Mr. Usher, because we're going to have to flip through the pages a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And my apologies to the Chamber. I misspoke. The book was published. No, I did not misspeak, the book was published in 2004. I'm just waiting for the e-court version to come up. Is there a problem? That is not quite the first page. There should be a title page. But we can start with this page, if you don't mind. Mr. Usher, if you could turn -- turn to the next page, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, we see on the second page a message from Mr. Boskoski. It says: "This modest contribution to the truth about Macedonia I dedicate to the immortals who with their blood confirmed their loyalty to their home land. To the defenders of Macedonia." Do you see that, Inspector?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then below that, above the signature of Mr. Boskoski, it says: "I do not acknowledge a battle for Macedonia without its triumph." If you turn to the next page -- actually, I'm sorry, Mr. Usher, the next page in English says, "My Battle for Macedonia," and then a subtitle, "Contribution to the clarification of the military conflict in Macedonia, 2001/2002." Mr. Usher, if we could turn to what is the third page. That's it; should be there. And this is page 5 in the English version. Can you turn perhaps one more page for the witness. There's poem there that hopefully you see, Inspector. It says: "Macedonia is my pain and joy." Do you see that? Could you turn one page over, please. Do you see that poem beginning there now: "Macedonia is my pain and joy."

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see my colleague is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are following the questions of my learned colleague the Prosecutor, and to be honest, I do not understand what is the purpose of those questions, so we would like to ask the Prosecutor why are we reading these sections from the book. And I think it would be also a correct, proper to ask the witness whether he had ever seen this book and whether he had ever read it, in order to continue asking the following questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this book is a memoir written by the accused regarding the events in 2001 and to a degree in 2002. And it's the Prosecution's intention to ask the witness some questions about certain parts of Mr. Boskoski's memoir, his version of the events during the conflict time relevant to the period of this indictment. I can certainly ask the witness whether he has seen the book before or not, but that is really the Prosecution's submission, Your Honour, neither here nor there. This witness was a member of the accused's close protection unit. He would have spent an inordinately amount of time with the witness during the crucial months of the summer of 2001 and I would like to explore with him several passages related to those events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may do so, Mr. Saxon, but will you do it with an eye to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are moving at a very cautious pace so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. If we can turn, please, to what you will see, Mr. Usher --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would just listen to the questions Mr. Saxon puts to you an answer those, that will be our most quick way of dealing with this matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you turn the page to the fifth page, excuse me, to the 15th page, and it is numbered now with page numbers. So can you turn to the -- where it says page 15 on the bottom. And this is at page 10 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you see, Inspector, at the bottom of page 15 it says: "I, Ljube Boskoski, already accepted by the people as Brother Ljube?"

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We could not get the answer. Could the witness move closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You need to move closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And speak louder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see the paragraph where it says, "I, Ljube Boskoski, already accepted by the people as Brother Ljube." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why was Minister Boskoski referred to as Brother Ljube? How did that come about, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't know. You should ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You have no idea why he was called Brat Ljube?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I guess, since he was close to the people, and that's why.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn, please, to the bottom of page 21 in the English version. And, Mr. Usher, this is page 42 in the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Inspector, you'll see in the middle of page 42 a paragraph and in the middle of the paragraph and this is an interview that was given -- Mr. Boskoski is describing an interview he gave in April of 2001. And do you see a sentence there where it says: "Yet I sent a message to them," and them in this case is the UCK, the NLA. "I sent a message to them again. There are no concessions." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you see in the next paragraph, the very first line and this for those following in English, this is the top of page 22, a sentence beginning: "This interview had a great impact on the public." Do you see that line?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During the spring of 2001, was Minister Boskoski receiving a lot of attention in the media in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: By the time you became part of Minister Boskoski's close protection unit, was the minister appearing a lot in the news, in the media, in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: To -- to quite a degree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn, please, in the Macedonian version to page 46, to page 23 of the English version. Inspector, you'll see on the left side of page 46 you see a paragraph saying: "I immediately set off for Tetovo." Do you see that line? Do you see the paragraph beginning with that line.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This paragraph reads: "I immediately set off for Tetovo." This was on the 16th of May, 2001. "I wanted to acquaint myself with the situation on the very spot. This became a regular practice for me, because I am a man who wants to observe the situation up close, and the security situation in the Republic of Macedonia at that time demanded that I be always with the Macedonian defenders in the field. That is, in the immediate focus of events. There, where the hoots of bullets next your own ears is a reality." Do you see what I've just read?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Minister Boskoski often go out to the battlefield areas?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn now to what is page 60 in the Macedonian version, and this will be page 29 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, on the left side of page 60 in the Macedonian version, and for those following in English this is at the bottom of page 29, there's a box and the box has a heading. It says,"Fourth Assassination Attempt." Do you see that? On the left side right here. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then it reads: "On the 3rd of June, in the vicinity of Matejce police station, while Minister Boskoski was getting information about the situation in this part of the front, machine-gun fire was opened on him and the group accompanying him. After the unsuccessful attempt, the terrorists undertook a fierce attack in order to eliminate him, yet the attack was defied by the Ministry of Interior guard and security units." Are you following with me?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you with Minister Boskoski that day, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: No, I don't recall this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Well, I would like to show you a video then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn away from the book for a moment, and if we can please view a clip from what is Rule 65 ter number 974. This is a video-clip from Macedonian television made around the 3rd of June, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Inspector, I would like you to watch this video closely, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, do you recognise the people now in this video that you can see here?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who do we see first in the foreground wearing the blue helmet?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Who is the person you see here wearing the helmet?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: The minister of interior, Ljube Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And just behind him, is that you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. So at least on this particular trip you were with the minister. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we continue the tape, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I would seek to tender that video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I can ask additional questions if the Chamber prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Our concern is to see how it is going to assist the case. What is its relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, the -- in the Prosecution's submission, Your Honour, the -- the fact that the minister of the interior, the accused Boskoski, went out into the field so often -- actually, what I need to do Your Honour, if I will give me some leave is ask perhaps a few more questions to further establish the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, what did Minister Boskoski do when he went out to the battle areas like this?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: As minister of the interior, normally he extended support to the police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, for example, how would Minister Boskoski do that? Who would he meet with on these trips?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I think he was in contact with everyone, regardless of rank and position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You're saying everyone within the police units?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: You asked me about on the ground, who could be there on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. But when you say he was in contact with everyone, regardless of rank and position, referring to people who are members of the police, the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did the members of these police units respond when Minister Boskoski came to visit them at the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: They carried out their tasks immediately and so to say, they cooperated. They worked with the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on -- on these visits, did you ever hear Minister Boskoski give instructions to the members of the police out at the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I have not seen that. Perhaps moral support.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the Prosecution's submission this video-clip is relevant to the issue of the effective control of the accused Boskoski over police units out in the field, and therefore, it is at least relevant to the matters in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, effective control should be established by the Prosecutor towards the executors of the acts for which is listed by the Prosecution in the indictment. Therefore, this proposal that the video-clip could in that direction give the response on the question of effective control is of no significance, absolutely of no significance. Secondly, when we talk about the general effective control, the witness was clear on this case. He had never heard on the battlefield the minister give orders and that mainly this was main -- moral support in question which in no way does not contribute to the clarification of the issue of effective control from the listed regions. Therefore, we objected to taking this exhibit as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P401, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to what is at page 63 in the Macedonian version, and it's the middle of page 31 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you'll see, Inspector, in the middle of page 63, in your version, a paragraph beginning with: "These were the days." Do you see that sentence, the middle paragraph. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is in the middle of page 31 in the English version. And this paragraph reads thusly: "These were the days in which I was working until the last atom in my body. My alertness and engagement could not be measured by 24 or 48 hours, but by series of nights and days without sleep. Yet with an unbreakable desire in the fight for Macedonia. Mainly, owing to my young age, stamina and my unshakeable Macedonian patriotism in which there is room for every human being, for all citizens of whatever ethnic or religious group if they sincerely and truly loved Macedonia." Do you see that, inspector?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you confirm that during that period of the spring, beginning of June 2001, Minister Boskoski was working very, very hard?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please. I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was it your impression that the minister in 2001, in the spring/summer of 2001 was working day and night?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. The paragraph ends: "In those sleepless nights and days, I became aware of the dangerous traps for the government with the military conflict being on top of all worries, which for the Macedonians in Macedonia and in the whole world had become a war for their fatherland from which there was no way back until the final victory and the final defeat of the terrorists and other enemies was achieved." Do you see what I've just read to you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At that time, Inspector, were you inspired by the activities, the dedication of Minister Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I do not understand the question. What do you mean "inspired"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you feel that Minister Boskoski was an inspiration to you and other members of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During that time, during the crisis months of the summer of 2001, were there police reservists mobilised?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't know. I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you another question. During the crisis time in 2001, were you aware that ethnic Macedonians, patriots volunteered to be reservists? Were you aware of that? Did you know people who did that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. If you go a little bit further down the page, Inspector, to the next paragraph you see a line that says: "So on 6th June 2001." Do you see that? The next paragraph, a few lines from the beginning, do you see the date 6th June 2001?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There it says: "On 6th June 2001, I had a statement for the journalists." And then, if you follow that along on the next page Inspector, later in that paragraph the statement says this: "We must not allow for the terrorists to lead us to the negotiation table and talk to them. To the question whether the high state officials were seriously considering to declare the state of war, I gave a moderate and decisive answer." And then the last line it says: "The terrorists enter Macedonia from Kosovo and the Macedonian security forces will act everywhere terrorist movement is noticed until they are completely destroyed." Do you see that, Inspector.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: No, no, I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you go to the top of page 64, please. Do you see at the top of page 64, it says: "We must not allow for the terrorists to lead us to the negotiation table." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then the last sentence, it says that: "the security forces will act everywhere terrorist movement is noticed until they are completely destroyed." The last sentence of that paragraph. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you hear Minister Boskoski express these beliefs in public during the summer of 2001?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did he express these beliefs to you?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In 2001, Inspector, did you know a man named Johan Tarculovski? Can you recall knowing Johan Tarculovski?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Very -- too little.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, can you recall how you knew him, even just a little?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Since he was my colleague, he worked in the Ministry of Interior. Otherwise, I have not had any personal contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall in 2001 ever seeing Johan Tarculovski with Minister Boskoski?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I do not understand the question. Where do you mean? Where do you mean have I seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For example, can you recall seeing Mr. Tarculovski and Minister Boskoski meeting, for example, in restaurants? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would it help you recall if I show you the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor a few years ago, where you talked about this? Would that help you recall?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: If I may clarify, perhaps I've said this in a context that they had met by chance, but meetings and sitting together, no. Because all wanted to greet Ljube at that time. Perhaps this is the context in which you understood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And would you see Johan Tarculovski greet Minister Boskoski at private places, like restaurants when you were with the minister?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, tell me, in 2001, did Johan Tarculovski have a reputation as a brave officer, a fighter?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know if Johan Tarculovski fought in combat during those crisis months?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't know this either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know whether Johan Tarculovski was a member of the Posebna unit during 2001?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm -- I was the security officer. I was not a member of this. Have you to ask others about this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall knowing a man in 2001 named Zoran Jovanovski who was also known as Bucuk?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of him too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you recall at that time what the man known as Bucuk did for a living?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would it help you to recall if I show you your statement from 2004 to the Office of the Prosecutor where you explained where this man known as Bucuk worked?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. Then we have copies of Inspector Jakovoski's statement in English and Macedonian. If a Macedonian version could be provided to the witness, please. And can you turn, Inspector, to paragraph 24 of your statement, please, in the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you assist him Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see paragraph 24 begins: "Being asked who else I know from Kometa which were present in Ljuboten, I can name Bucuk Jovanovski." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now does that refresh your recollection as to where the man known as Bucuk worked?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In 2001, where did the man known as Bucuk work? Bucuk.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: In the Kometa agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And can you recall the names of other persons who also worked or were associated with the Kometa agency in 2001?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I cannot recall at this time. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you take a look at paragraph 24 again. It says: "Being asked who else I know from Kometa which were present in Ljuboten, I can name Bucuk Jovanovski, Johan Tarculovski, Sasa, the one who was wounded, the brother of the wounded, Vlatko Janevski, former department chief of the Kometa. These ones I can identify." Does that help refresh your memory, Inspector?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, but I cannot remember now who this Vlatko is and Sasa is. I have not seen them for seven years at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But time when you made this statement this information was correct, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall seeing Minister Boskoski and Bucuk and Johan Tarculovski together during the crisis times of 2001?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I cannot recall this either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would it help you to look at a part of your statement where you describe this? Would that help you recall, refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I told you that I can't at this moment remember seeing them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's exactly why I'm asking, Inspector, can I assist you by asking to you look at paragraph 34 of your statement, please. Paragraph 4 says: "Being asked when I have seen the last contact between Bucuk and Johan, I can't tell anything of official context, but I want to explain that I have seen on multiple occasions before the events all three persons, the minister, Bucuk and Johan meeting on private occasions as they were going to the same places. I have seen contacts in places, restaurants like Fufo, Galija, Dzino, when I accompanied the minister on private occasions before the events." Do you see that, Inspector?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Does that help refresh your memory now?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Surely they must have seen each other. I don't know to pinpoint the number but everybody sees everybody in Skopje; it is a small town. And in these places where people frequent, we all see each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Tell me something, back in 2001, this man known as Bucuk, was he known as a brave man, a fighter?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn now to what would be paragraph -- excuse me, page 67 of the Macedonian version of the book written by Minister Boskoski, and this is at page 33, Your Honours, of the English version. And at this page, if you take a look at the second paragraph, Inspector, in the middle of the page, here Minister Boskoski is describing the events undertaken by the Macedonian security forces against the terrorists in Aracinovo. Do you see that, the very middle of the page, middle of page 67? "Everything was ready to undertake the Macedonian security forces decisive actions against the terrorists in Aracinovo." Do you see that, Inspector, that line?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then it say this, the next sentence: "The only thing we were waiting for was the order from the state highest officials and the crisis management coordination body. I did not agree with the indecisive views of this body which were pushing Macedonia into negotiations with the terrorists, something that the great Albanian national chauvinist centres truly wanted. I made up my mind. I resigned my membership from this body and proposed Refet Elmazi in my place." Do you see that, Inspector?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At that time when Minister Boskoski resigned from the crisis management coordination body for the reasons that he explained, were you proud of him, you and your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe the witness should be asked first whether he knows at all that the minister resigned from this coordination body so that he could be asked the following question then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you aware, Inspector, that the minister resigned from the coordination body in protest of the indecisive policies of certain members?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can take a look at what is page 69 of your version. It's a chapter beginning with "The people's response." This is the bottom of page 33 of the English version. And here Minister Boskoski is describing the actions of the security forces in Aracinovo. Do you see that first paragraph there, Inspector?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can the inspector's second microphone be turned on, please..

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: A little ways down in that paragraph it says: "So they went ahead and the "they" are the members of the security forces. "So they went ahead to defend Macedonia and its capital Skopje by crying out, Everything for Macedonia." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When I was encouraging them and seeing them off into the fire, they were saluting me with "everything for Macedonia." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This salute, "Everything for Macedonia," what did it mean and why did the police officers use it to the minister?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Firstly, I have to say that I do not remember this being said, this statement. And secondly, of course if someone lives in Macedonia he would be for Macedonia, not for any other state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Can we move on, please, to what is page 72 in the Macedonian version, and it's page 35 in the English version. Can you recall, Inspector, the end of June 2001, there were demonstrations in the city of Skopje, people were upset because the NLA had been allowed to pull out of the village of Aracinovo. Do you recall those demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you recall providing protection to the minister when he went to see those demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: During that time, I was not there. I was in Croatia as a guard to the minister's family, and this is why I can't say anything about this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Then I will move on. If we can, please, can we move to page -- let me -- on the 10th of August, 2001, eight Macedonian soldiers were killed in a mine explosion at a place called Ljubotenski Bacila. Can you recall -- Do you recall hearing about that? It was Friday, the 10th of August, eight Macedonian soldiers were blown up. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can, please, show the witness what is 65 ter 188, please. And this should be for Your Honours, tab 6 in your binders. It would be tab 6 in the Inspector's binder, please. If he can be shown the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see, this is a news report, Inspector, it says, "FYROM Security Council convenes 10th August, supports firm action." Do you see that at the top?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's a report from 10.00 p.m., 2200 hours Greenwich time on the 10th of August, reporting that the Security Council of the Republic of Macedonia held a meeting, which focussed on the country's current security and political situation and resulted in the adoption of a number of specific conclusions. And then it says: "The Security Council paid tribute to the Macedonian security forces servicemen who were killed near the Skopje village of Ljubanci and expressed deep regret and sympathy to their families." And then it say this: "At last night's meeting, the council concluded that the firm action should resume to eliminate any threat to the security forces and to the citizens of the Republic of Macedonia." Do you see what I've just read, Inspector?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall, did you accompany Minister Boskoski -- excuse me, did you escort Minister Boskoski to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I was never at the Security Council, I was a body-guard. I'm not ... it's like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that the Prosecutor should first ask the witness whether he had ever seen this information, whether he knows at all that the council was convened and only then to proceed with asking further questions because he is a body-guard and not a member of this body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I was on my way to doing that, Your Honour. I think I have gotten part of the response that I asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you aware that after the mine explosion that killed eight Macedonian soldiers that the Security Council called for firm action to be taken?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know, were you with Minister Boskoski when he received the news about the killing of the eight Macedonian servicemen?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me just tell you that I never had such contact with the minister, that the minister would tell me what decisions were brought by the Security Council or any such important information, so I could not reply to this question either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, I asked you a very different question and I'd like a response, please. My response was this -- my question was this: On the 10th of August, 2001, were you with Minister Boskoski when he received the news that eight Macedonian soldiers had been killed at Ljubotenski Bacila?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't recall, and, secondly, the minister never told me any such thing that they were killed. That police officers were killed in Ljubanci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please return to Mr. Boskoski's book; this is at tab 1 of your binders. And can we turn, please, to page 103 in the Macedonian version. This is a separate section, Your Honour, you will see a -- you will see a sticker for the first 48 pages of your binder. First 48 pages of tab 1. If you would turn now, please, to the second sticker, which bears ERN number N000-9659. The English translation is just over two pages. And there's a subtitle called "Cuckoo Eggs," to help you identify this portion. Inspector, I'd like to direct your attention, please, to the second paragraph below the title, "Cuckoo Eggs." And it says this: "On August the 10th, 2001, one more tragedy occurred." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "Which only strengthed the feverish pace imposed by the terrorists before the signing of the Ohrid Framework Agreement. In the Ljubotenski Bacila/Ljuboten Sheepfolds locality - Skopje area, there was once again a terrorist ambush. Eight members of the army of the Republic of Macedonia were killed and as much were heavily and lightly injured by land-mines, rocket launchers and automatic weapons." Are you following with me?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it says: "The Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Ministry of Defence undertook a joint operation to break up the terrorist group which operated in that area. Battles were waged in the Skopje area for two days already. In the official communique of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, we have emphasised that in the armed clash of the joint security forces of the Republic of Macedonia conducted on August 11th and 12th in Ljuboten village, in the zone of Skopje, against the paramilitary armed grouping the NLA terrorist, five perpetrators were killed." Have you been following with me, Inspector?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the 10th, Friday, the 10th, Saturday, the 11th of August, 2001, were you present when the Minister Boskoski discussed these -- this so-called joint operation, to break up the terrorist group?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I have to say again that nothing was discussed with me regarding such issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would move for the admission of 65 ter 4, this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we never disputed the authenticity of this book, but considering that this is a book as a whole, our proposal is for the entire book to be received in evidence, if it is received, and not just individual chapters that we have today here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason the Prosecution has not previously translated the entire book relates to CLSS policy, not Prosecution policy. It is simply that CLSS has told the Prosecution that they do not have the resources to translate entire books and so they have -- CLSS has always strongly encouraged the Prosecution then to select certain portions of books, such as this, for translation. If the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive those parts of the book that are presently tendered. If is thought by either Defence that some other parts are material to the issues in this case, they will, in the course of their cross-examination or cases identify those additional parts. So we will receive ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm informed that the whole of the original work is in fact in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the English language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, the original book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the translations are of limited parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive the work in that form in which it is presently in e-court. In other words, the whole of the Macedonian book and that part of it which is translated. If reliance is intended to be placed on any part which is presently only in Macedonian, then that will need to be specifically raised in cross-examination with the witness and translations provided into English in due course, if it is thought that there are material passages in the Macedonian version which have not been translated into English. So it will be received on that basis.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P402, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, rather than starting another major topic now, would it be appropriate to take the first break at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon. We will adjourn now and resume at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, I'd like to ask you, please, to turn your mind to the morning of 12th of August, 2001. Can you recall what you did on that morning?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: This was a long time ago, but I could recall that we were constantly going to the battle grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would it help you to refresh your memory to look at the statement you gave several years ago where you describe what you did on that morning, please? If you take a look at what is paragraph 12. Paragraph 12 says: "On Sunday, I was starting my work at 0800. Myself, Medarov, Laste, and Branko Pejcinovski were on duty this day. We have a room in the cabinet where the body-guards are located. From there we were going to pick up the minister. I think it was 08.15 when we were picking him up on this Sunday morning. On this day, we were using two cars. One car was black, armoured Jeep Cherokee. The other one was a black Chrysler car. We were going to the cabinet at around 0830. The minister went inside and we were waiting in our room, the room which is right to the room for the Minister of Interior. Then we were leaving the Ministry of Interior. The next station we went was a hairdresser in Skopje, in the area of Madzari. We arrived at around 10.00. The shop was especially opened for the minister. The owner is a friend of the minister. I was inside with the minister, and I remember that he received a call from President Trajkovski. I don't know the content of the conversation which was spoken. I only heard that the minister addressed the name President. Therefore, I say it was a conversation with President Trajkovski. We were leaving after half an hour. The next destination was Volkovo village near Skopje. We stopped in the middle of the village at around 11.00 and we stayed for around 15 minutes. The minister spoke with the relatives of people who died in the conflict. I don't know who these persons were. Afterwards, we were going directly from Volkovo to Ljubanci. The minister told the driver to go now to Ljubanci next." Inspector, does this help to you refresh your memory about what you did on that Sunday morning?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I can say that up to a point the text is correct, and that I can recall that we went to Volkovo. As for having been to Volkovo, either I have not understood the person who questioned me or it was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Is there anything else that is not correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: When this deposition was being taken, when I was giving my statement I said that I cannot recall a lot of it, and now, six years after even more. Therefore, I cannot say with certainty whether this is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Can you recall driving with Minister Boskoski to Ljubanci on the 12th of August, that Sunday?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall approximately what time you and Minister Boskoski arrived in Ljubanci?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Around 12.00 noon, 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall where in Ljubanci you and the minister and others, if there were more people, stopped?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: We stopped in front of a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you and the minister get out of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you stopped in front of the house and got out of the vehicles, where did you and the minister go?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: In the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inside the house itself, or was it the compound that included the house?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: In the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. And from that courtyard, could you observe the village of Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: From somewhere close to the courtyard, could you observe the village of Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I could not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to that in a little while. Can you recall approximately how long you and Minister Boskoski remained at that house in that courtyard?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: An hour and 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall who was present in the courtyard when you and the minister entered?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I can only say that when we entered the courtyard, the minister met with the head of -- of that municipality, of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you recall who else was present when you entered the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I did not see anyone else I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that. I asked you if you can recall whether there were other persons present. Can you recall that, Inspector?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, yes. There were uniformed police officers in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall approximately how many such uniformed police officers in camouflage uniforms were there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I cannot say what their number was. I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you turn, please, to what is paragraph 17 in your statement, Inspector. Take a look, Inspector, at the middle of paragraph 17. It says: "We were going to a stone table in the garden. In the moment when we arrived were around 50 people in police uniforms in the garden. They were wearing green camouflage police uniforms." Does that help to refresh your memory as to how many such police officers there were?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: In the statement I have said the number. This is not approximately correct. Perhaps there were 100, perhaps there were 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Can you recall what those police officers were doing when you and the minister entered the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: They stood still and greeted the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You say they stood still. What do you mean by that? Does that mean they stood up or they stood at attention? I don't know what that means.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: They stood at attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall who the commander of this group of police officers was standing there at attention?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I do not recall. And I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you take a look at the middle of paragraph 17 that is in front of you, Inspector, several years ago you told an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor: "Being asked who the commander of this unit was, I say the commander of the police officers was Zoran Jovanovski, Bucuk. Jovanovski came to the minister to the stone table and they both spoke about the situation in the village." The next sentence is confusing. It was a typed conversation between the minister and Jovanovski. "I was at the moment at some two metres from the minister away. I could understand from the conversation that they were talking about the situation in the village and that it was not completely under control. According to the conversation, I understood that or understand that Jovanovski told the minister that there was shooting coming from nearly all houses in Ljuboten." Does this help refresh your memory about what you saw and heard in that courtyard on the 12th of August, Inspector?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Last time and now I tell you again, while I was giving the statement, at that time also to the investigator I said that I do not recall to the best of my ability who the minister met with there. But now if I were to think about it, if I were to think through it, I recall that at the stone table the one person he met was the head. I don't recall his name, first name or last name, and he spoke with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, do you recall seeing a second group of men -- actually, I'd like you, before we go on, can you turn, please and perhaps the usher can help us, to page 10 of your statement in the Macedonian version, 10th page. Page 10. Can you turn the page, go to the next page, please. Next page, please. Next page, please. Next page. Next page. Next page. Next page. Should be the second-to-the-last page. It says -- that should it be it right there. You see it, there's a page there, Inspector, it says: "Witness Acknowledgment." Do you see that, Inspector?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It says that: "This statement has been read over to me in the Macedonian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection. I have given this statement voluntarily and I am aware that it may be used in legal proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal for the Prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international law committed in the territory of the Former Yugoslavia since 1991, and that I may be called to give evidence in public before the Tribunal." Do you see your signature there, Inspector?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is it still your testimony today, under oath, that you do not recall the name of the person who Minister Boskoski spoke with at that stone table?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: In this Court, I gave my solemn oath that I will speak the truth and nothing but the truth. The truth is what I'm telling you now, and then in front of the investigator I said that I did not recall. However, since I was held for over eight hours and I was very tired, and he wanted to hear from me that this name should be Zoran Jovanovski and Johan Tarculovski there and this is what I said, this is why. Secondly, it was because at that moment, another party was in power, another government was in power, which could dismiss me from work, could fire me from work and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, is it your testimony here today that the OTP investigator who interviewed you forced you to give these details about Zoran Jovanovski and Johan Tarculovski? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: No, they did not force me. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But what?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: The truth, which I'm saying now, is the truth now. And this is that Minister Boskoski saw only with the head at that stone table.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, do you recall seeing a second group of police officers arrive in that courtyard on the 12th of August?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps I saw. I cannot recall at this moment. I cannot recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, can you assist us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, I'd like to ask you to try to refresh your memory by looking at paragraph 20 of your statement. Take a look at paragraph 20 and about the third sentence it says: "At this time I didn't see Johan Tarculovski in the yard, he came later. I have not seen with my own eyes Johan Tarculovski coming together with a wounded person. I saw only Johan Tarculovski, he was wearing a police uniform. The wounded person was Sasko or Saso or Aleksandar, last name Janevski. Being asked if I know this person, I say I don't know him but heard Johan Tarculovski telling this to Zoran Jovanovski. This conversation happened around three hours after arrival. All together we were around three hours in the yard, and I monitored this from a distance of around five metres. I don't know what happened to the person and whereabouts of the wounded person, but I think they took him to the hospital. I think he was wounded in the leg, but as I said before, I never saw the person. Johan came with a group of around 15 people in uniform. They were wearing camouflage uniforms. They were sitting down together with the people in the yard." Inspector, does that help refresh your memory about seeing a second group of police officers in that courtyard that day?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: At the onset I said that Johan Tarculovski, I do not know him personally. Even if I were to see him now, I would not recognise him. Then and now, I could not recognise him that he was coming with that second group. Therefore, I cannot say that Johan Tarculovski came there. Yes, a group came, but whether Johan was there or not, I cannot say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, about an hour ago, perhaps a bit longer, you told this Trial Chamber, again under oath, that you knew Johan Tarculovski in 2001. You knew him as a member of the ministry's security and protection. Is it really your testimony now before this Court, under oath, that you did not know him? Is that really what you're telling this Chamber, under oath?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: This is how it is, sir. I'm speaking under oath and this is the truth. Personally, I said I do not know him. It's different to know someone or to have heard about someone. This can be interpreted in two different ways. That is to say, I had heard of Johan Tarculovski, that he worked in the Ministry of Interior. This means that I do not exactly know what he looks like. So, therefore, I cannot say whether he came or not. This would be guessing at this moment, if I were to say that I truly saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, the passage of testimony that I referred to earlier is at page 19, lines 11 to 13 of the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall that some weapons were brought to that courtyard. Can you recall that, in Ljubanci?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you take a look at paragraph 21, please, of your statement. Paragraph 2 reads: "I don't know the origin of these weapons. I think they were brought by Johan Tarculovski's group. A second group of Johan was still in the village when we left. Being asked why I'm saying that the weapons were brought by Johan's group, I can say that I only know that his group was in Ljuboten. I think that at the moment when Johan spoke with Zoran, Bucuk, also the weapons, the ID cards and the other things visible on the video were brought in front of the house, but I haven't seen this." Does this refresh your memory, Inspector, as to who brought the weapons to that courtyard?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: In my statement, Your Honour, I say, I can see having said here that I have not seen this with my own eyes. For this whole time I am claiming that I have not seen any of this, that I do not know and that I do not recall. Therefore, I cannot say also about the weapons, I cannot say that I have seen it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you take a look at the next paragraph of your statement, Inspector, you told an OTP investigator several years ago in a signed statement: "I know Johan Tarculovski since around five years. Johan was body-guard of Boris Trajkovski and after this, he was the body-guard of the wife of Trajkovski." Then you said: "I met Johan during my work in the police." Inspector, you are testifying under oath today. I ask you again: Did you see Johan Tarculovski in that courtyard on the 12th of August, 2001?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Sir, I shall repeat once again. I know that I'm testifying under oath and thank you for reminding me of this. And, once again, I will repeat that I do not recall Johan Tarculovski in the second group that came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall whether there was anyone from the Kometa security company present in the courtyard on that day?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: As you know, I work in the Ministry of Interior, not in Kometa. Therefore, I do not know the people who work there, and I could not say and point out ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, to help you refresh your memory, could you please take a look at paragraphs 23 and 24 of your statement. Paragraph 23 says: "Zoran Jovanovski, I know for a longer time than Johan, I think more ten years." Paragraph 24 says: "Being asked who else I know from the Kometa which were present in Ljuboten, I can name Bucuk Jovanovski, Johan Tarculovski, Sasa, the one who was wounded, the brother of the wounded, Vlatko Janevski, former deputy chief of the Kometa. These ones I can identify. The people I named are the most important ones. These people were in a responsible position. Vlatko and Johan were not in the garden. All these people were wearing police uniforms on this day." Does that help refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Again, I will say that I do not know anyone from the Kometa agency personally. I know them from pictures, from hearsay. Therefore, I cannot say anything on this matter and on this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, I'd like to show you a video. Can we please show what has been marked for identification as Exhibit P363. And if you could pay attention, Inspector, please. Pay attention to the commentary, Inspector, that is being given here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This is video footage taken from the house in Ljubanci looking towards Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001, received from Macedonian television.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Stop. Stop. Can we go back a little bit, please. Well, let's go forward for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Stop. Can we stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, is that you that we see here?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we keep going, please. This is at 13:45 on the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, you listened to the voice of the journalist on that broadcast, right, did you hear what she said?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was there anything that the journalist said that you disagree with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll let the witness answer the question first, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please repeat the question. I do not understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was there anything that the journalist said that was incorrect?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Well, I'm not the one who should assess the veracity of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, can you tell us whether you heard anything said that was wrong or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I have no comment with regards to this question. I don't know. I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but you had already decided about this video because on the list of the Prosecution's witnesses, there is actually the one witness who made this clip, and that witness should be questioned about the content of that story. In my opinion, it would be correct to ask this witness only about individual occurrences whether he had witnessed those, rather than commenting story of a journalist. But the witness has already answered, so I have no further remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I make one further remark, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you need to, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then I will move on, if I'm trying the patience of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Inspector, the journalist who you heard speaking there is a woman named Eli Cakar; do you know who she is?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't know her.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you remember a television journalist accompanying Minister Boskoski to Ljubanci that day?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Sir, I can only state that I was interested in the minister and not the journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. A moment ago you mentioned that when you gave your statement to the OTP several years ago, another political party was in power and that you said certain things to avoid being fired. Do you remember when you told us that a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you have any concerns about your professional position now, given that a different political party is in power?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Do I have to answer this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Does the fact that the VMRO party is now in power influence the way you have testified today?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: No, not in the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions at this time. I would like to inform the Chamber that I erred at transcript page 26, line 17, where I mentioned 65 ter number 188. I should have said 65 ter number 118, and I'm grateful to my colleagues for catching my mistake, as they usually do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jakovoski. I am Edina Residovic, and with my colleague Guenael Mettraux, I defend Mr. Ljube Boskoski. Before I ask you some questions, Mr. Jakovoski, I would like to ask you once more to wait a little when I ask a question, wait for the question to be interpreted into Macedonian and English, so that the Chamber and my colleagues in this courtroom be able to follow what I ask and what you answer. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before you were employed by the Ministry of Interior in 1990, you graduated from a gymnasija secondary school in Skopje. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that you enrolled at the faculty of physical culture where you did not graduate from the faculty as a whole but only the first two -- you only finished the first two years. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After two years of attending the faculty, you went to serve in the Yugoslav People's Army. You were a conscript in the -- to serve your mandatory military service. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After your military service, you were unemployed for five years practically. You had no job at all. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And it was completely clear to you that it was very difficult to find employment, because many young people at the time were unemployed. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: It is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me when I say that even now in the Republic of Macedonia many people are unemployed and that jobs are difficult to find; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Answering the questions of my learned friend the Prosecutor, you said that you worked in the police in 1990 as a uniformed police officer. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: That is correct, uniformed police officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And as a uniformed police officer, you first worked at Karpos police station for two years and then from 1993 to 1997 you worked at Bit Pazar police station. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Both these police stations are in the city of Skopje and belong to the sector of security of the city of Skopje. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While working as a police officer in uniform, you did your duty in accordance with the law, law about the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from your duties as laid down by the law, you and other police officers also acted upon the orders of your superiors at the time. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were working at the Karpos and Bit Pazar police stations, your immediate superior was the police station commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So that as a police officer you immediately executed orders received from the commander of the police station, or by a person authorised by him; that is, a deputy or somebody else from the police station. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the commander of the police station was the person responsible for the situation in that police station. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA JAKOVOSKI
utterances.text: It is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If a uniformed police officer from that station or a third person who would come there would -- would do something wrong, something against the law, or go beyond their authority, overstep their authority, then the person in charge would establish all relevant facts and launch disciplinary proceedings against that police officer.
